Recombinant DNA Technology

Engineering Life: Tools and Principles for Modern Medicine

screens.title: Imagine a Living Bio-Factory
screens.html:
Imagine a Living Bio-Factory

How do we produce life-saving insulin for millions of diabetics, or growth hormones for children with endocrine disorders?

We don't 'manufacture' these complex proteins in a traditional factory. Instead, we reprogram bacteria to build them for us. This is the power of recombinant DNA (rDNA) technology.

screens.title: Recap: PCR Amplification
screens.html:
QUICK REVIEW

Recap: PCR Amplification

PCR uses thermal cycling to create millions of copies of a specific DNA sequence.

Denaturing: Heat (95°C) splits DNA strands.

Annealing: Primers bind to target ends (55°C).

Extension: Taq polymerase adds bases (72°C).

screens.title: Recap: Gel Electrophoresis
screens.html:
QUICK REVIEW

Recap: Gel Electrophoresis

Once amplified, we use Gel Electrophoresis to verify and separate our DNA fragments.

Remember: DNA is negatively charged and moves toward the positive electrode. Smaller fragments navigate the agarose mesh faster than larger ones.

screens.title: Defining Recombinant DNA
screens.html:
🔑

Defining Recombinant DNA

What is rDNA?

Recombinant DNA is DNA that has been formed artificially by combining constituents from different organisms.

By 'pasting' a human gene into a bacterial plasmid, we create a hybrid molecule that never existed in nature.

Key point

Because the genetic code is universal, a bacterium can read a human gene and produce the exact same protein.

screens.title: The Four Main Stages
screens.html:
The Four Main Stages

Creating recombinant DNA is a systematic process. We follow these four critical steps:

Isolation

Use restriction enzymes to cut the target gene.

Insertion

Place the gene into a vector, such as a plasmid.

Transformation

Move the recombinant plasmid into a host cell.

Selection

Identify cells that successfully took up the gene.

screens.title: KEY CONCEPT
screens.html:
KEY CONCEPT

Stage 1: Isolation

To isolate a gene, we use Restriction Enzymes (endonucleases). These enzymes recognise specific palindromic sequences.

Some enzymes create 'blunt ends', but for rDNA, we prefer 'sticky ends'—overhanging single-stranded sequences that easily bond with matching pieces.

screens.title: The Importance of Vectors
screens.html:
The Importance of Vectors

A vector is a DNA molecule used as a vehicle to artificially carry foreign genetic material into another cell.

Why Plasmids?

Small, circular DNA separate from the main chromosome.

Easy to manipulate in a lab.

Replicate independently within the host.

screens.title: The Cutting Strategy
screens.html:
The Cutting Strategy

Critical Rule

To insert a human gene into a plasmid, you must use the same restriction enzyme for both.

This ensures the 'sticky ends' on the human DNA are perfectly complementary to the 'sticky ends' on the opened plasmid.

screens.title: Analyzing Enzymes
screens.html:
Analyzing Enzymes

You can use two different restriction enzymes to cut the gene and the plasmid as long as they both produce sticky ends.

👍​

TRUE

👎​

FALSE

Now it's time to explain why...

screens.title: Analyzing Enzymes
screens.html:
Analyzing Enzymes

You can use two different restriction enzymes to cut the gene and the plasmid as long as they both produce sticky ends.

👎​

Why is that?

a) Different enzymes would destroy the DNA backbone entirely, preventing any further ligation.

b) Different enzymes produce different base sequences at the sticky ends, meaning they won't be complementary and cannot bind together.

Answers on the next slide...

screens.title: Analyzing Enzymes
screens.html:
Analyzing Enzymes

You can use two different restriction enzymes to cut the gene and the plasmid as long as they both produce sticky ends.

👎​

✅​

Why is that?

a) Different enzymes would destroy the DNA backbone entirely, preventing any further ligation.

b) Different enzymes produce different base sequences at the sticky ends, meaning they won't be complementary and cannot bind together. ✅​

screens.title: Stage 2: Insertion & Ligation
screens.html:
🧠

Stage 2: Insertion & Ligation

Once the gene and plasmid are mixed, they join via base-pairing at their sticky ends. However, this bond is weak.

DNA Ligase is the 'glue' that makes the join permanent. It creates covalent bonds in the sugar-phosphate backbone.

Remember

Restriction enzymes cut; DNA Ligase pastes.

screens.title: KEY CONCEPT
screens.html:
KEY CONCEPT

Stage 3: Transformation

Transformation is the process of getting the recombinant plasmid into the host bacterial cell.

Bacteria aren't naturally 'eager' to take up foreign DNA. We make them competent using techniques like heat shock (alternating hot and cold) or electroporation.

screens.title: The Efficiency Problem
screens.html:
The Efficiency Problem

Transformation is inefficient; only 1 in 10,000 bacteria take up the recombinant plasmid, resulting in three cell types:

Untransformed - Bacteria that took up no plasmid.

Non-Recombinant - Bacteria that took up a plasmid lacking the human gene.

Recombinant - Our success: bacteria carrying the plasmid with the target gene.

screens.title: Stage 4: Selection
screens.html:
🔍

Stage 4: Selection

How do we find our 1-in-10,000 success? We use Antibiotic Resistance Genes as markers.

The vector plasmid contains a gene for resistance to an antibiotic (e.g., Ampicillin). We grow the bacteria on agar containing that antibiotic.

Example

If a bacterium didn't take up the plasmid, the antibiotic will kill it. Only transformed cells survive.

screens.title: Cloning & Expression
screens.html:
Cloning & Expression

Once we have identified our recombinant bacteria, we let them do what they do best: multiply.

Every time the bacterium divides, it replicates the recombinant plasmid. This is called gene cloning. Eventually, the bacteria translate the gene into the desired protein.

screens.title: Case Study: Human Insulin
screens.html:
Case Study: Human Insulin

Human insulin was the first medication produced using rDNA (approved in 1982). Before this, insulin was extracted from the pancreases of slaughtered cows and pigs, which caused allergic reactions in some patients.

Advantages

Pure human protein (no allergies).

Infinite supply (bacteria grow fast).

Cheaper to produce at scale.

screens.title: Biotechnology in Western Australia
screens.html:
Biotechnology in Western Australia

In Australia, recombinant technology is vital for producing vaccines like Hepatitis B and hormones like EPO (Erythropoietin) for kidney patients. It is a cornerstone of the modern pharmaceutical industry and a key part of your ATAR syllabus.

Exam Style Question

What is the primary reason for using the same restriction enzyme on both the human DNA and the bacterial plasmid?

1.

To ensure both DNA samples have the same electrical charge for electrophoresis.

2.

To produce complementary sticky ends that can form hydrogen bonds.

3.

To prevent the bacteria from digesting the new plasmid.

4.

To speed up the function of DNA ligase during the cooling phase.

screens.title: Thinking Critically
screens.html:
Thinking Critically

Ethics and Safety

While rDNA can solve healthcare crises, it also raises questions. What if an engineered bacterium escaped into the wild?

This is why lab strains are often 'crippled'—they are engineered to be unable to survive outside a specific lab environment with special nutrients.

screens.title: Mastering the Process
screens.html:
Mastering the Process

Restriction enzymes are used to ____ target genes, which are then joined to plasmids using ____. The process of inserting these plasmids into bacteria is called ____.

Word bank 🏦​

transformation, isolate, polymerase, ligase, separate, electrophoresis

Answers on the next slide...

screens.title: Mastering the Process
screens.html:
Mastering the Process

Restriction enzymes are used to isolate target genes, which are then joined to plasmids using ligase. The process of inserting these plasmids into bacteria is called transformation.

Word bank 🏦​

transformation, isolate, polymerase, ligase, separate, electrophoresis

✅​

screens.title: Summary: The Flow
screens.html:
Summary: The Flow

Step 1

Isolation of gene and vector using same restriction enzymes.

Step 2

Ligation: sticky ends join to form recombinant DNA.

Step 3

Transformation: Host cells take up the recombinant plasmid.

Step 4

Selection and Cloning: Grow recombinant cells to produce protein.

screens.title: Class Discussion
screens.html:
Class Discussion

The universal nature of the genetic code allows bacteria to produce human proteins. In what ways might this technology be limited when dealing with more complex proteins that require 'post-translational modifications' (changes made to proteins after they are built)?

screens.title: Class Discussion
screens.html:
Class Discussion

You might have said...

Bacteria lack organelles like Golgi bodies, preventing complex protein

glycosylation. Human proteins may also misfold or prove toxic to

bacterial hosts. Consequently, scientists often use yeast or mammalian

cell cultures to produce complex proteins instead of bacteria.

✅​

questions.title: Written practice
questions.prompt: A human protein is to be made using bacteria. Explain why the coding sequence, regulatory sequences and host cell must all be suitable.
steps: Use an intron-free coding sequence, such as cDNA made from mature mRNA, because bacteria do not splice human pre-mRNA.
Include a promoter and other regulatory elements recognised by the bacterial host so the gene can be expressed.
Choose a host and production process able to produce and recover the required functional protein.

o: DNA from different sources has been combined
It has been destroyed by heat
bank.why: Recombinant DNA combines DNA sequences from different sources.

bank.q: Why is a suitable promoter needed?
o: It enables transcription in the host
bank.why: The host needs appropriate regulatory sequences to transcribe the inserted gene.

bank.q: Why can a human gene require a cDNA version for bacterial expression?
o: Bacteria do not splice human introns from pre-mRNA
bank.why: cDNA made from mature mRNA lacks introns, avoiding a processing step bacteria do not perform.
